new_statements.quote: [p.50] ... lexical items other than verbs, retain their underlying tone in the surface form. While stress and intonation patterns may affect the perceived tone, such changes are not contrastive. Clause-final particles such as the interrogative marker su and the assertive marker si may carry high, mid or low tone, depending on the tone of the preceding morpheme, intonation, stress patterns, and other factors. [p.53] Relative high tone on the verb codes perfective aspect, while in all other aspects the verb carries its underlying tone. Intonation, stress, and neighboring tones may affect, and sometimes supersede, the tone of a given morpheme. [ch.1 §6.1] [Pévé] has three tones, high, mid, and low, which carry functions in the domains of both lexicon and grammar.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pévé is described as a three-tone language (H, M, L; lexical tone plus grammatical H tone for perfective). Stress is mentioned only as a non-contrastive factor that can perturb perceived tone; the grammar (as far as every indexed passage shows, and per Lovestrand's review of its thin phonology chapter) gives no rule for where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author flags tonal variation and possible toneless grammatical particles as needing further research (p.50, p.53).
new_statements.domain_note: Remarks concern surface tone of morphemes/clause-final particles in connected speech; no word-level stress domain is defined. Text obtained only as verbatim Google Books search snippets (saved), not from a held copy of the book.
new_statements.identity_note: Shay 2019 describes Pévé as spoken around the Chad-Cameroon border (data from one speaker, Lazare Wambadang, elicited in Maroua) = peve1243 proper. Sachnine 1982 describes Lamé / vùn dzèpàò of Cameroon, which Glottolog lists as dialect lame1268 under peve1243 but which Shryock 1997 (p.33) classes as the southernmost dialect of Heɗe (herd1234-type, ISO hed); WALS 'Lamé' [lam] and UPSID/PHOIBLE 'LAME' are built on Sachnine. Venberg 1975 describes Peve of Chad (Lutheran Brethren mission area).

sources.citation: Shryock, Aaron. 1997. The classification of the Masa group of languages. Studies in African Linguistics 26(1): 29-62. DOI 10.32473/sal.v26i1.107396.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Says tone is lexical on nouns and marks verbal aspect in Masa-group languages (p.43). Treats Lamé (Sachnine 1982) as the southernmost dialect of Heɗe rather than of Peve (p.33).
